strengths: The paper addresses an important question: why adversarially trained models can retain good clean accuracy while exhibiting a large robust generalization gap. Studying learning dynamics is a useful complement to sample-complexity and representation-complexity explanations.

The signal/noise decomposition in Sections 3–4 makes the proposed mechanism interpretable. The quantities U and V provide concrete measures of shared feature learning and sample-specific memorization.

The experiments examine input-space sensitivity across perturbation radii and training epochs on MNIST and CIFAR-10. The reported CIFAR-10 train/test divergence provides qualitative motivation for investigating localized robust fitting.
weaknesses: The central result does not establish robust overfitting under a consistent worst-case threat model. Theorem 4.1 guarantees low training error only on fixed GTA examples generated using the oracle signal direction and patch location, whereas test robustness is evaluated over the entire perturbation ball. GTA leaves all noise patches unchanged, directly enabling the proposed memorization mechanism. No approximation guarantee connects this attack to the learned network's inner maximization. Consequently, the result does not establish that worst-case robust training error is small.

The proof of the main generalization result contains substantive mathematical gaps. In Theorem C.12, sums of cubic Gaussian projections are treated as sub-Gaussian, although nonzero cubic Gaussian polynomials generally have heavier tails. The same proof infers that every noise-weight component has constant Euclidean norm from V_i(T) = Θ(1); bounds on these training-projection sums do not establish such norm bounds. Both steps support the clean-test guarantee and require a valid replacement argument.

The construction proving Theorem 5.2 need not retain the claimed Ω(1) robust test error. Assumption 5.1 permits a distribution on two well-separated labeled points with a vulnerable clean separator. Once both points appear in training, the constructed f_S robustly classifies the entire population. Under the standard worst-case interpretation of robust training error, no classifier with zero robust training error can have positive robust test error in this example. An assumption ensuring sufficient uncovered probability mass is missing.

Theorem 7.1 is false under its stated assumptions. A constant-logit classifier has zero input gradient, but with nondegenerate label proportions its empirical logistic risk can fall below its population risk with probability approximately one-half, even with smooth input densities. The proposed bound allows no gap in this case. Appendix E also produces additive density-estimation errors that are not justified as being absorbed into the gradient-only bound. Additionally, Proposition 7.2 concerns robust versus clean population risk, which is different from the train–test generalization gap.

The representation-complexity contribution is overstated relative to its quantifiers and prior work. Theorem 5.3 is an existential worst-case lower bound, not a general exponential requirement under Assumption 5.1. Its construction remains linearly separable, so the claimed extension of Li et al. (2022) to the larger neural-separable class does not clearly add a substantive lower-bound result. This existence argument also does not establish a preference of gradient descent for CGRO classifiers.

The empirical evidence does not identify the proposed mechanism. Flatness within the training radius and increased sensitivity elsewhere do not uniquely demonstrate signal/noise decomposition or memorization through local indicators, and the flatness–gap correlation does not establish causality. Direct tracking of U and V in the theoretical model and controlled comparisons of attack strength would provide stronger evidence. Training/evaluation attack settings, the procedure for maximizing gradient norms, and variability across runs are insufficiently specified for reproduction.
